live_web_research.page_text: [2610.22496] Scaling Online Exploration for Robot Agents Skip to main content Search arXiv Press Enter to search · Advanced search --> Computer Science > Robotics arXiv:2610.22496 (cs) [Submitted on 15 Oct 2026] Title: Scaling Online Exploration for Robot Agents Authors: Runhan Huang , Xiangcheng Zhang , Haoyu Chen , Yitong Li , Yen-Jen Wang , Bohan Lyu , Haotian Ye , Chuye Hong , Yixuan Wang , Chloe Su , Haoyu Xiong , Yangzhen Wu , Enze Xie , Travis Manderson , Stefano Ermon , Pieter Abbeel , Antonio Torralba , Dawn Song , Weirui Ye , Yilun Du View a PDF of the paper titled Scaling Online Exploration for Robot Agents, by Runhan Huang and 19 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Robot learning has advanced by scaling demonstration datasets and model capacity; however, deploying a new robot embodiment or task typically necessitates a dedicated teleoperation corpus. The resulting policies remain bounded by their imitation distributions, limiting generalization and continual self-improvement. We introduce RAX (Robot Agent eXploration), an open-source framework for robot agents centered on scaling exploration: enabling agents to improve by acquiring online experience and synthesizing executable programs. In RAX, a general-purpose coding agent generates robot control code, operating without action demonstration data, hand-engineered action primitives, or value-function guidance. Through online exploration, the agent identifies decision sequences that achieve task goals and compiles them into modular programs encapsulating the full perception-planning-control loop. Using RAX, we present a systematic multi-embodiment study on scaling online exploration across precision and long-horizon manipulation tasks using single-arm, bimanual, dexterous, mobile, and humanoid systems in simulation and on real robots. Generalization performance on unseen environments improves consistently as exploration scales. In simulation, RAX outperforms top baseline models by +37.4% on average. On real robots, RAX autonomously learns memory-dependent, articulated, high-precision, deformable, and long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks without human demonstrations, continually improving performance by composing verified skills from prior exploration sessions. As exploration scales, we observe emergent capabilities including active perception, error recovery, safety guardrails, and human-robot collaboration. We open-source RAX as a generalist robot-agent platform in which new robot embodiments are integrated through their APIs alone, without teleoperated data collection or policy training. Real-robot sessions Each video is one full session. The agent explores on the real robot, fixes its own mistakes, and turns what works into programs. No demonstrations, no teleoperation, no policy training. The raw logs of every session, with the agent's transcripts, robot tool calls, state logs and camera recordings, are on Hugging Face . Simulation Prior SOTA RAX Method A frozen LLM coding agent drives the robot through its perception and control interfaces. What it learns lives in its workspace: notes, programs and verified skills. Exploration compiles into code 241 × faster on the air fryer Agent, 72 min Fully automated program by RAX, 18 s 103 × faster on the Bandu tower Agent, 17 min Fully automated program by RAX, 10 s Contribute your robot's skills Every skill a RAX agent learns on a real robot is an executable procedure, stored with its preconditions, checks, failure modes and the runs that verify it, so a later session on another robot can reuse and compose it. The RAX skill library collects them, one library per embodiment, starting with the Rainbow RB-Y1 and the Franka FR3. If your agent has learned a task on a real robot, please contribute it: add the skill to your robot's library by following the contributing guide , or bring a new robot with its own library . Case studies Robot rollout sessions 3D model built by the agent No model of the air fryer was given. From what it measured in its first manual run, the agent wrote an articulated model, a fixed body and a drawer on a prismatic joint, placed it on the point cloud of each new scene, and planned its actions on it. In RAX, a general-purpose coding agent generates robot control code directly, operating without action demonstration data, hand-engineered action primitives, or value-function guidance. Through online exploration, the agent identifies decision sequences that achieve task goals and compiles them into modular programs encapsulating the full perception-planning-control loop for fast inference. Using RAX, we present a systematic multi-embodiment study on scaling online exploration across fine-grained precision and long-horizon manipulation tasks using single-arm, bimanual, dexterous, mobile, and humanoid systems in simulation and on real robots. Deep summary ⚡ AI-generated The problem A robot can copy a demonstration without learning how to adapt For many learned robots, a new task begins with teleoperation : a person controls the machine remotely while the system records what the person did. A model trained to imitate those recordings can perform familiar motions, but each new robot or task often needs its own examples. That collection effort is expensive, and the resulting policy —the learned rule for choosing actions from what the robot sees—can still fail when a scene changes in a way the recordings did not cover. The trouble is not only that a cup, drawer, or tool has moved. A longer task may require the robot to discover how to connect several familiar actions, or how to recover when the first plan fails. A policy that was trained to copy a fixed set of actions has no natural way to diagnose those misses and rewrite its own strategy. This paper asks whether the robot can learn from the kind of practice people use: try an action, inspect what happened, and improve the next attempt. Its answer is RAX, a system that lets an AI coding agent explore through the robot’s controls and turn successful discoveries into programs. The central question Can a robot discover useful skills from its own attempts instead of needing a new teleoperation dataset for each task? The trade-off is whether limited, costly practice can produce code that adapts to new scenes well enough to replace replaying demonstrations. The gap More demonstrations do not give a robot a way to discover That dependence on recorded examples leaves a gap between acting and learning. Vision-language-action systems map images and instructions to robot actions, while world-action models also predict how a scene may change; both improve by training on demonstrations, so a new robot body commonly needs data of its own. They can generalize within their training distribution, but the paper argues they do not provide a process for learning new strategies from experience gathered during evaluation. Language models have also been used to plan robot tasks or write programs. Those systems often act once or with only a few examples, while newer interactive coding-agent approaches have tended to focus on narrower settings or retain some dependency on demonstrations, offline trajectories, policy training, or a simulator built from the real workspace. RAX takes a different scaling axis: the robot gathers more experience for itself, without updating the language model or training a robot policy. The paper’s central claim is therefore about the form of learning. If the agent’s discoveries become executable, testable code rather than weights that hide a policy’s reasoning, then it can inspect failures, repair only the affected step, and reuse successful skills. RAX at a glance Research question Can online robot practice replace task-specific action datasets? The goal is self-improvement from interaction, not a new robot policy trained on demonstrations. What learns Programs, notes, and verified skills The coding agent’s underlying AI model stays fixed. What it receives Task text, robot tools, observations, and a limited number of attempts Goal images or demonstrations vary by benchmark; HumanoidArena supplies three demonstrations per task. What it produces An observation-driven program It checks conditions and outcomes instead of replaying a recorded trajectory. How it is tested Unseen scenes across six simulation benchmarks and real robots Some benchmarks evaluate standalone programs; others retain the agent in the loop. The idea RAX turns its attempts into a program that can act without the model RAX answers the discovery gap by changing what the agent keeps. A task begins with a general-purpose coding agent—an AI that can inspect images, run code, and use tools—acting directly through the robot interface. The agent can observe a scene, issue a motion, read the result, and decide whether to try again; its task knowledge accumulates in a workspace rather than in updated model weights. This is the loop represented in the hero diagram: perception and control feed the agent, the agent writes a robot program, and memory preserves notes and skills for later work. Programs call the same interface as the agent, so the code it tests during exploration can later run on its own. From a first attempt to a reusable skill 01 Explore Try the task through the robot’s tools The agent starts from task instructions, the available goal images, sensors, and a fixed number of task attempts (episodes). It uses small actions and fresh observations to learn what the task requires. 02 Measure Build only the world model the task needs Color and depth can form a 3D map of objects and surfaces. The agent may use robot geometry, or kinematics, to relate joint positions to hand poses, and add force checks when the interface supports them. 03 Compile Turn a working decision into checked code A program observes, plans, acts, and tests preconditions—the conditions that must already be true—and outcomes. The agent rehearses it on new exploration scenes and repairs the stage that fails. 04 Keep Save verified skills with their conditions A skill is a reusable program paired with notes about when it applies and evidence that it ran successfully. Later sessions can retrieve and compose those skills. A real air-fryer example makes the code concrete. The agent measures the direction in which a drawer pulls and uses vertical to define a perpendicular axis in its task frame—a small coordinate system for expressing target positions: $$t = z \times d$$ Here $z$ is vertical and $d$ is the measured pull direction; their cross product $t$ gives a perpendicular direction for positioning and clearance checks. This is a task-specific geometry rule from one example, not a universal RAX equation. Fig. 2 . A depth point cloud—a 3D map made from measured surface points—anchors a moving fryer model; planned paths then open its drawer and place objects without replaying one fixed arm trajectory. The drawing shows why a compiled program is more than a memorized sequence: it estimates where the fryer sits, models the drawer moving along its measured pull direction, and plans several actions against that model. In this run, it opened the drawer by 13.1 cm and checked the basket rim against a new measurement; the predicted and measured rims differed by 6.5 mm. These numbers describe one real task, while the broader claim is that agents can write such perception and planning logic from their own exploration. The system A shared tool boundary carries the same learning loop across robots For those programs to work on different robots, RAX separates task reasoning from the machinery that moves each body. The agent writes code for perception, planning, and checks; a robot-specific backend—the hardware-side software stack—exposes sensors and controls through a tool interface and retains low-level control and safety checks. The agent can act only through that boundary, so its program cannot rewrite the drivers or bypass the robot’s limits. That division lets the same learning workflow connect to single-arm and bimanual arms, dexterous hands, a mobile household robot, and a humanoid. The tools differ because the bodies differ, but the agent still explores, records what worked, and makes a tested program. Bringing up a new robot design therefore requires an interface and its documentation, not a new teleoperation corpus or policy-training run. The paper’s measurements are not entirely learned from scratch: each session receives instructions and platform skills, and some benchmarks supply task-completion images. The important distinction is that those images show the goal rather than the action sequence—except HumanoidArena, where three teleoperated demonstrations are available to the exploring agent. Benchmark evidence Online exploration beats demonstration-trained baselines across unlike tasks Portability only matters if exploration produces reliable behavior beyond one robot and one scene. The main simulation studies test that claim on new layouts: RAX explores within an episode budget, submits a program or a frozen workspace, and is then measured on benchmark eval

selected_records.title: Scaling Online Exploration for Robot Agents

article.body:
RAX turns robot exploration into executable task programs

RAX, an online-exploration framework, was tested across simulated systems and two real robots: the Franka FR3 and Rainbow RB-Y1. The paper does not specify their joint counts or payload capacities. In a documented real-robot session, the agent modelled and opened an air-fryer drawer. A coding agent generated control code and explored through the robot’s interfaces, without human action demonstrations, teleoperation or policy training; disclosed training hours and dataset sizes are absent.

The authors describe autonomous learning and recovery during real-robot sessions. The evidence is physical demonstrations, not sustained deployment: it establishes specific task learning under test conditions, not reliability across homes or workplaces.
